1. Polynomial regression for bike rental data

In this problem, we consider modelling the number of rides each hour for a bike rental company. The raw data are stored in the file bike_rental_hourly.csv, which can be downloaded from the Canvas page of the course1.

The dataset contains 17379 hourly observations over the two-year period January 1, 2011 - December 31, 2012. The dataset contains many features that may be useful for predicting the number of rides, such as the hour of the day, temperature, humidity, season, weekday, etc. In this section, we consider modelling the logarithm of the number of rides as a function of the time of the day (scaled to the interval [0,1], see below). The following code reads in the data (note that you have to change to the path were you stored the file!) and creates the variables of interest (log_cnt and hour).

Problem 1

bike_data$log_cnt <- log(bike_data$cnt) #create column log_cnt and attribute log of column cnt to it

The number of rides seem to peak in the morning (8 AM \(8/23 \approx 0.35\) ) and after work (6 PM \(18/23 \approx 0.78\)).

We start by fitting a polynomial of order 2 to a training dataset consisting of Feb 1, 2011 - March 31, 2011. We use the following two months (April 1, 2011 - May 31, 2011) as test dataset to evaluate the predictions. The following code creates the training and test datasets.

Step 2: Create the training and test datasets

bike_data_train <- bike_data[bike_data$dteday >= as.Date("2011-02-01") & bike_data$dteday <=  as.Date("2011-03-31"), ]
bike_data_test <- bike_data[bike_data$dteday >= as.Date("2011-04-01") & bike_data$dteday <=  as.Date("2011-05-31"), ]

The following code estimates the model (a polynomial of order 2) using least squares and computes the root mean squared error (RMSE) for both the training data and the test data. Moreover, the code plots the training data, test data and the fitted polynomial in the same plot.

Problem 1.1

Fit a polynomial of order 8 using least squares, without using R functions such as lm(). Plot the training data, test data and the fitted polynomial in the same plot.

Step 3: Estimate the model using least squares method

y_train <- bike_data_train$log_cnt
y_test <- bike_data_test$log_cnt
p <- 8 # Order of polynomial

#Design matrix of features 
x_train <- cbind(1, poly(bike_data_train$hour, p, raw = TRUE, simple = TRUE)) 

#Find coefficient
beta_hat <- solve(t(x_train)%*%x_train)%*%t(x_train)%*%y_train #t(x_train) = transpose of x_train

# Predict in-sample and compute RMSE
y_hat_train <- x_train%*%beta_hat
RMSE_train <- sqrt(sum((y_train - y_hat_train)^2)/length(y_train))
cat("RMSE_train", RMSE_train,"\n")
RMSE_train 0.7232024 
# Predict out_of_sample and compute RMSE
x_test <- cbind(1,poly(bike_data_test$hour, p, raw = TRUE, simple = TRUE))
y_hat_test <- x_test%*%beta_hat
RMSE_test <- sqrt(sum((y_test - y_hat_test)^2)/length(y_test))
cat("RMSE_test", RMSE_test,"\n")
RMSE_test 1.021449 
# Plot training data, test data, and fit on a fine grid.
plot(log_cnt ~ hour, data = bike_data_train, col = "cornflowerblue", ylim = c(0, 8)) #create a scatterplot showing how log_cnt varies across hours based on the training data 
lines(bike_data_test$hour, bike_data_test$log_cnt, type = "p", col = "lightcoral") #add a graph type p - point (scatter plot) to the existing scatterplot, based on test data
hours_grid <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 1000) #create 1000 points from 0-1, to feed into the line graph, to create a smoother curve
x_grid <- cbind(1, poly(hours_grid, p, raw = TRUE, simple = TRUE))
y_hat_grid <- x_grid%*%beta_hat
lines(hours_grid, y_hat_grid, lty = 1, col = "black") #fit the line
legend(x = "topleft", pch = c(1, 1, NA), lty = c(NA, NA, 1), col = c("cornflowerblue", "lightcoral",  "black"), legend=c("Train", "Test", "Fitted curve"))

Problem 1.2

Fit polynomials of varying order 1-10 using least squares, without using R functions such as lm(). Compute the RMSEs for the training and test data and plot them on the same figure as a function of the polynomial order. Are you underfitting or overfitting the data?

To fit polynomials of varying order 1-10, we can use a loop for p.

orders <- 1:10
RMSE_train_vec <- numeric(length(orders)) #create a vector to store RMSE_train
RMSE_test_vec <- numeric(length(orders))  #create a vector to store RMSE_test

for (p in orders) {
  # Predict in-sample
  x_train <- cbind(1, poly(bike_data_train$hour, p, raw = TRUE, simple = TRUE))
  beta_hat <- solve(t(x_train) %*% x_train) %*% t(x_train) %*% y_train
  y_hat_train <- x_train %*% beta_hat
  RMSE_train_vec[p] <- sqrt(mean((y_train - y_hat_train)^2))
  
  # Predict out_of_sample
  x_test <- cbind(1, poly(bike_data_test$hour, p, raw = TRUE, simple = TRUE))
  y_hat_test <- x_test %*% beta_hat
  RMSE_test_vec[p] <- sqrt(mean((y_test - y_hat_test)^2))
}

# This cat is different as I want to display the vector vertically
cat("RMSE_train_vec:\n") 
RMSE_train_vec:
for (val in RMSE_train_vec) {
  cat(val, "\n")
}

0.7232024

cat("RMSE_test_vec:\n")

for (val in RMSE_test_vec) {

# Plot RMSEs
plot(orders, RMSE_train_vec, type = "b", col = "blue", ylim = range(c(RMSE_train_vec, RMSE_test_vec)),
     xlab = "Polynomial Order", ylab = "RMSE", main = "RMSE vs Polynomial Order")
lines(orders, RMSE_test_vec, type = "b", col = "red")
legend("topright", legend = c("Train RMSE", "Test RMSE"), col = c("blue", "red"), lty = 1, pch = 1)

As the polynomial order increases, both training and test RMSE decrease, and the test RMSE eventually levels off. There is no clear sign of overfitting, since test RMSE does not increase at higher polynomial orders — it simply plateaus. This suggests that model complexity beyond a certain point brings diminishing returns, but not evident overfitting.

Overall, we have 3 scenarios:

  • Underfitting: Both train and test loss function is high

  • Good fit: Both train and test loss function is low

  • Overfitting: Training loss is low/decreasing, while test loss is high/increasing, they may cross paths, and the test loss can decrease and then increase after 1 point (begins to overfit).

Problem 1.3

Polynomials are global functions and their fit may be sensitive to outliers. Local fitting methods can sometimes be more robust (less affected by outliers). One such method is the loess method, which is a nonparametric method that fits locally weighted regressions to subsets of points and subsequently combines them to obtain a global fit. Use the loess function in R with the standard settings to fit a locally weighted regression to the training data. Is this method better than that in Problem 1.1? Plot the training data, test data and both fitted curves in the same plot.

The predict() function can be used on the object returned by loess().

# Fit loess model to training data
loess_fit <- loess(log_cnt ~ hour, data = bike_data_train)

# Predict on training and test data
y_hat_loess_train <- predict(loess_fit, newdata = bike_data_train)
y_hat_loess_test <- predict(loess_fit, newdata = bike_data_test)

# Compute RMSE for loess
RMSE_loess_train <- sqrt(mean((bike_data_train$log_cnt - y_hat_loess_train)^2))
RMSE_loess_test <- sqrt(mean((bike_data_test$log_cnt - y_hat_loess_test)^2))

# COPY OF 1.1

y_test <- bike_data_test$log_cnt
p <- 8 # Order of polynomial

#Design matrix of features

beta_hat <- solve(t(x_train)%*%x_train)%*%t(x_train)%*%y_train #Find coefficient, t(x_train) = transpose of x_train

plot(log_cnt ~ hour, data = bike_data_train, col = "cornflowerblue", ylim = c(0, 8)) #create a scatterplot showing how log_cnt varies across hours based on the training data

2. Regularised spline regression for bike rental data

Using the same training and test datasets as above, we will fit spline regressions with L1 and L2 regularisations (also known as penalties).

We create a natural cubic spline basis function for the variable hour with 25 equally spaced knots between 0.05 and 0.95. We first fit a regression using least squares without regularisation. The following code does this and plots the spline fit together with the training and test data. Note that we are not adding an intercept to the design matrix, since this is taken care of by the argument intercept=TRUE.

suppressMessages(library(splines)) # Load the library splines
knots <- seq(0.05, 0.95, length.out = 25) # Creates 25 equally spaced knots between 0.05 and 0.95

x_train <- ns(bike_data_train$hour, knots = knots, intercept = TRUE) # Constructs natural cubic spline basis matrices for the hour variable in training data - ns creates splines basis 
x_test <- ns(bike_data_test$hour, knots = knots, intercept = TRUE) # Constructs natural cubic spline basis matrices for the hour variable in test data
beta_hat <- solve(t(x_train)%*%x_train)%*%t(x_train)%*%y_train # Fits the spline regression using least squared

# Plot training data, test data, and spline fit on a fine grid (similar to problem 1, already explained)
plot(log_cnt ~ hour, data = bike_data_train, col = "cornflowerblue", ylim = c(0, 8)) 
lines(bike_data_test$hour, bike_data_test$log_cnt, type = "p", col = "lightcoral")
hours_grid <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 1000)
X_grid <- ns(hours_grid, knots = knots, intercept = TRUE) # cbind(1, ns(hours_grid, knots = knots))
y_hat_spline_grid <- X_grid%*%beta_hat
lines(hours_grid, y_hat_spline_grid, lty = 1, col = "lightcoral")
legend(x = "topleft", pch = c(1, 1, NA), lty = c(NA, NA, 1), col = c("cornflowerblue", "lightcoral",  "lightcoral"), legend=c("Train", "Test", "Spline"))

We have deliberately chosen too many knots and no regularisation so that the fit has a large variance, which is clearly evident from the figure above. Your task in the next problem is to fit a regularised spline regression.

Problem 2.1

Fit a spline regression to the training data with an L2 regularisation using a suitable value of \(\lambda\), without using R functions such as glmnet(). Plot the fit together with the training and test data.

Tip

The least squares estimator when using an L2 penalty is known as the Ridge regression estimator. Moreover, to determine a suitable value of \(\lambda\), one approach is to fit several models (using different \(\lambda\) values, e.g. lambda_grid <- seq(0, 1, length.out=100)) and choose the value of \(\lambda\) that minimises the root mean squared error of the test data.

\(\lambda >0\) is the regularization parameter, it controls how much we penalize large coefficients. To find a suitable value of \(\lambda\) , we need to try out a bunch of them (100), and then find the lambda that gives the lowest RMSE. To do this, we can use a loop to try out those values

# Create lambda values to try out
lambda_grid <- seq(0, 1, length.out=100)

# Create vectors to store RMSE values
RMSE_test <- numeric(length(lambda_grid))
RMSE_train <- numeric(length(lambda_grid))

#Create identity matrix with dimension = ncol in x_train
matrix_I <- diag(ncol(x_train))

# Loop over lambda values to compute ridge regression estimates and RMSEs
for (i in seq_along(lambda_grid)) # seq_along: Generates a sequence of integers from 1 to the length of lambda_grid 
  {
  lambda <- lambda_grid[i]
  
  # Ridge regression estimator: (X'X + λI)^(-1) X'y
  beta_ridge <- solve(t(x_train) %*% x_train + lambda * matrix_I) %*% t(x_train) %*% y_train
  
  # Predict on train data
  y_hat_train <- x_train %*% beta_ridge
  RMSE_train[i] <- sqrt(mean((y_train - y_hat_train)^2))
  
  # Predict on test data
  y_hat_test <- x_test %*% beta_ridge
  RMSE_test[i] <- sqrt(mean((y_test - y_hat_test)^2))
}

# Find the lambda that gives the lowest RMSE
best_lambda <- lambda_grid[which.min(RMSE_test)] # which.min return index of the smallest RMSE in that vector

# Fit final model using best lambda
beta_ridge_best <- solve(t(x_train) %*% x_train + best_lambda * matrix_I) %*% t(x_train) %*% y_train

# For self-check
cat("best_lambda", best_lambda, "\n") # for self-check
best_lambda 0.01010101 
cat("min(RMSE_train)", min(RMSE_train), "\n")
min(RMSE_train) 0.6911984 
cat("min(RMSE_test)", min(RMSE_test), "\n")
min(RMSE_test) 1.006595 
# Plot training data, test data, and fitted spline curve
plot(log_cnt ~ hour, data = bike_data_train, col = "cornflowerblue", ylim = c(0, 8))
lines(bike_data_test$hour, bike_data_test$log_cnt, type = "p", col = "lightcoral")

# Predict on a fine grid for smooth curve
hours_grid <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 1000)
x_grid <- ns(hours_grid, knots = knots, intercept = TRUE)
y_hat_grid <- x_grid %*% beta_ridge_best

# Add fitted curve to plot
lines(hours_grid, y_hat_grid, lty = 1, col = "darkgreen")
legend(x = "topleft", pch = c(1, 1, NA), lty = c(NA, NA, 1),
       col = c("cornflowerblue", "lightcoral", "darkgreen"),
       legend = c("Train", "Test", "Ridge Spline"))

Problem 2.2

Use the package glmnet to fit a spline regression with an L2 regularisation using the same basis functions as the previous problem. Find the optimal \(\lambda\) by applying the one-standard deviation rule when cross-validating the training data using 10 folds. Compute the RMSE (using the optimal \(\lambda\)) for the training and test data. Plot the fit together with the training and test data.

Tip

The help() function will be very useful here. Another useful function is cv.glmnet(), where cv stands for cross-validation. The argument alpha (to the cv.glmnet() function) is key. Finally, the predict() function can be used on the object returned by cv.glmnet() and the argument s (to the predict() function) controls which \(\lambda\) to use.

Both add a penalty term (controlled by λ), but the form of the penalty differs:

L2(Ridge) uses the square of the coefficients, shrinks all coefficients smoothly toward 0, adds bias, reduces variance smoothly, exactly to 0

Closed-form solution: \(\hat{\beta} = (X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1} X^\top y\)

L1 (Lasso) uses their absolute value, Forces some coefficients exactly to 0, Adds bias, but can simplify model by removing variables.

suppressMessages(library(glmnet))
# Fit ridge regression using cross-validation function in glmnet
set.seed(0)
cv_fit_L2 <- cv.glmnet(x_train, y_train, alpha = 0, nfolds = 10) #alpha = 0: L2 penalty only

#str(cv_fit_L2) # For self-check

# Extract optimal lambda using one-standard deviation rule
lambda_best_L2 <- cv_fit_L2$lambda.1se
#lambda.1se: The largest λ within one standard error of the minimum cross-validated error

# Predict in-sample using optimal lambda
y_hat_train <- predict(cv_fit_L2, newx = x_train, s = lambda_best_L2)
RMSE_train <- sqrt(mean((y_train - y_hat_train)^2))

# Predict out-of-sample using optimal lambda
y_hat_test <- predict(cv_fit_L2, newx = x_test, s = lambda_best_L2)
RMSE_test <- sqrt(mean((y_test - y_hat_test)^2))

cat("lambda_best_L2", lambda_best_L2, "\n") 
lambda_best_L2 0.4378188 
cat("RMSE_train", RMSE_train, "\n") 
RMSE_train 0.7111962 
cat("RMSE_test", RMSE_test, "\n")
RMSE_test 1.000773 
# Plot training data, test data, and fitted spline curve
plot(log_cnt ~ hour, data = bike_data_train, col = "cornflowerblue", ylim = c(0, 8))
points(bike_data_test$hour, bike_data_test$log_cnt, col = "lightcoral")

# Create a fine grid for smooth curve
hours_grid <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 1000)
x_grid <- ns(hours_grid, knots = knots, intercept = TRUE)
y_hat_grid <- predict(cv_fit_L2, newx = x_grid, s = lambda_best_L2)

# Add fitted curve to plot
lines(hours_grid, y_hat_grid, col = "darkgreen", lwd = 1)

# Add legend
legend("topleft", legend = c("Train", "Test", "L2 Spline Fit"),
       col = c("cornflowerblue", "lightcoral", "darkgreen"),
       pch = c(1, 1, NA), lty = c(NA, NA, 1), lwd = c(NA, NA, 2))

RMSE for train and test data in 2.2 and 2.3 are different, but by a very small gap. It’s safe to say they are similar. However, when choosing a model, using \(\lambda\).1se is more simple, as it tends to include fewer features, due to more regularization.

# Add fitted curve to plot
lines(hours_grid, y_hat_grid, col = "purple", lwd = 2)

# Add legend
legend("topleft", legend = c("Train", "Test", "L1 Spline Fit"),
       col = c("cornflowerblue", "lightcoral", "purple"),
       pch = c(1, 1, NA), lty = c(NA, NA, 1), lwd = c(NA, NA, 2))
Problem 2.2 RMSE_train 0.7111962  RMSE_test 1.000773 
Problem 2.4 RMSE_train 0.6913233  RMSE_test 1.005145

The RMSE in 2.2 and 2.4 are comparable. As the number of features used in this case is low (1), L2 could be a better fit, as it shrink, but not drop any coefficients to 0.

3. Regularised regression for bike rental data with more features and data

We now consider the full dataset and use many more features. We use the first one and a half years (Jan 1, 2011 - May 31, 2012) of data for training and the last half year (June 1, 2012- Dec 31, 2012) for testing.

We will use the following categorical features:

  • weathersit: Clear (1), cloudy (2), light rain (3), heavy rain (4).

  • weekday: Sun (0), Mon (1), Tue (2), Wed (3), Thu (4), Fri (5), Sat (6).

  • season: Winter (1), spring (2), summer (3), fall (4).

We will use the common approach in statistics that creates \(K-1\) dummy variables for a categorical variable with \(K\) levels. The first level is the reference category. The following code constructs these so called one-hot encodings and adds them to the dataset bike_data.

# One hot for weathersit
one_hot_encode_weathersit <- model.matrix(~ as.factor(weathersit) - 1,data = bike_data) # create a matrix with one column per level of weathersit
one_hot_encode_weathersit  <- one_hot_encode_weathersit[, -1] # Remove reference category
colnames(one_hot_encode_weathersit) <- c('cloudy', 'light rain', 'heavy rain')
bike_data <- cbind(bike_data, one_hot_encode_weathersit) # Add the new dummy variables to the original bike_data dataframe.

# One hot for weekday
one_hot_encode_weekday <- model.matrix(~ as.factor(weekday) - 1,data = bike_data)
one_hot_encode_weekday  <- one_hot_encode_weekday[, -1] # Remove reference category
colnames(one_hot_encode_weekday) <- c('Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu', 'Fri', 'Sat')
bike_data <- cbind(bike_data, one_hot_encode_weekday)

# One hot for season
one_hot_encode_season <- model.matrix(~ as.factor(season) - 1,data = bike_data)
one_hot_encode_season  <- one_hot_encode_season[, -1] # Remove reference category
colnames(one_hot_encode_season) <- c('Spring', 'Summer', 'Fall')
bike_data <- cbind(bike_data, one_hot_encode_season)
# Prepare the data sets
bike_data_train_3 <- bike_data[bike_data$dteday >= as.Date("2011-01-01") & bike_data$dteday <=  as.Date("2012-05-31"), ]
bike_data_test_3 <- bike_data[bike_data$dteday >= as.Date("2012-06-01") & bike_data$dteday <=  as.Date("2012-12-31"), ]

Problem 3.1

Fit a spline regression to the training data with an L1 regularisation. Find the optimal \(\lambda\) by applying the one-standard deviation rule when cross-validating the training data using 10 folds. Compute the RMSE (using the optimal \(\lambda\)) for the training and test data. For the spline, use the splines package in R to create natural cubic splines basis functions of the variable hour with 10 degrees of freedom, i.e. use the ns() function with df=10 as input argument. Moreover, set intercept=FALSE and add it manually to your design matrix instead.

The following variables should be included in the regression:

  • Response variable: log_cnt.

  • Features: hour (via the cubic spline described above), yr, holiday, workingday, temp, atemp, hum, windspeed, and all the dummy variables created above.

Tip

First create the design matrix of interest (you have to exclude the original variables you did the one-hot coding for). When creating the spline basis for the test data, you will need to use the same knots as when constructing the basis functions for the training dataset. If the spline is stored in a variable spline_basis, you can extract the knots by using knots<-attr(spline_basis, "knots") and then use the knots argument when constructing the design matrix for the test data, e.g. ns(bike_all_data_test$hour, df=10, knots=knots, intercept = FALSE).

y_train3 <- bike_data_train_3$log_cnt
y_test3 <- bike_data_test_3$log_cnt

# Construct natural cubic spline basis matrices for the hour variable in training data
x_train3_hour <- ns(bike_data_train_3$hour, df = 10, intercept = FALSE) 
knots <- attr(x_train3_hour, "knots")
x_test3_hour <- ns(bike_data_test_3$hour, df = 10, knots = knots, intercept = FALSE)

# Construct design matrices (combine other features, including one-hotted ones)
x_train3 <- cbind(
  1,  # Manual intercept
  x_train3_hour,
  bike_data_train_3[c('yr', 'holiday', 'workingday', 'temp', 'atemp', 'hum', 'windspeed', 'Spring', 'Summer', 'Fall', 'Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu', 'Fri', 'Sat', 'cloudy', 'light rain', 'heavy rain')]
)

x_test3 <- cbind(
  1,
  x_test3_hour,
  bike_data_test_3[c('yr', 'holiday', 'workingday', 'temp', 'atemp', 'hum', 'windspeed', 'Spring', 'Summer', 'Fall', 'Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu', 'Fri', 'Sat', 'cloudy', 'light rain', 'heavy rain')]
)

# Fit L1 regression
set.seed(0)

cv_L1_3 <- cv.glmnet(as.matrix(x_train3), y_train3, alpha = 1, nfolds = 10, intercept = FALSE)

# Select lambda using one-standard deviation rule
lambda_1se <- cv_L1_3$lambda.1se
cat("lambda_1se", lambda_1se, "\n")
lambda_1se 0.01797346 
# Predict in-sample
y_hat3_train <- predict(cv_L1_3, newx = as.matrix(x_train3), s = lambda_1se)
RMSE_train <- sqrt(mean((y_train3 - y_hat3_train)^2))
cat("RMSE_train", RMSE_train, "\n")
RMSE_train 0.7284213 
# Predict out-of-sample
y_hat3_test <- predict(cv_L1_3, newx = as.matrix(x_test3), s = lambda_1se)
RMSE_test <- sqrt(mean((y_test3 - y_hat3_test)^2))
cat("RMSE test", RMSE_test, "\n")
RMSE test 0.7113729 
# Predict on grid for plotting 
hours_grid <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 1000)
hour_spline_grid <- ns(hours_grid, df = 10, knots = knots, intercept = FALSE)

# Create dummy feature matrix for plotting (use average values)
x_grid <- cbind(
  1,
  hour_spline_grid,
  matrix(colMeans(x_train3[, -c(1:11)]), nrow = 1000, ncol = ncol(x_train3) - 11, byrow = TRUE)
)

y_hat_grid <- predict(cv_L1_3, newx = x_grid, s = lambda_1se)

# Plot
plot(log_cnt ~ hour, data = bike_data_train_3, col = "cornflowerblue", ylim = c(0, 8))
points(bike_data_test_3$hour, bike_data_test_3$log_cnt, col = "lightcoral")
lines(hours_grid, y_hat_grid, col = "purple", lwd = 2)
legend("topleft", legend = c("Train", "Test", "Lasso Fit (λ.1se)"),
       col = c("cornflowerblue", "lightcoral", "purple"), pch = c(1, 1, NA), lty = c(NA, NA, 1))

Problem 3.2

Which three features in Problem 3.1 seem to be the most important?

Tip

To explore which variables are most important, you can re-estimate the model in Problem 3.1 without cross-validation (using glmnet()). Note that you can apply the plot() function to an object returned by glmnet() using the arguments xvar="lambda" or xvar="norm", and label="TRUE", which allows you to visualise the lasso path.

To decide which features are more important, we can look at coefficient paths to see which become non-zero first

library(plotmo)
Loading required package: Formula
Loading required package: plotrix
set.seed(0)
# Fit L1 model without CV
L1_without_CV <- glmnet(as.matrix(x_train3), y_train3, alpha = 1, intercept = FALSE)

# Plot coefficient paths as lambda changes = how each feature’s coefficient changes as the regularisation strength (λ) varies
plot_glmnet(L1_without_CV, xvar = "norm", label = TRUE)
# Extract the name of top 3 features
coef_mat <- as.matrix(L1_without_CV$beta) #create matrix of all coefficients
first_nonzero_index <- apply(coef_mat, 1, function(row) which(row != 0)[1]) # look through each row of coef_mat, grab the index of the first non-zero beta
# Sort features by when they first become non-zero
sorted_features <- sort(first_nonzero_index, na.last = NA)  # remove features that never enter

# Get the names of the top 3 earliest features
top3_early_features <- names(sorted_features)[1:3]
print(top3_early_features)
[1] "hum"       "atemp"     "windspeed"

Problem 3.3

Carry out a residual analysis in Problem 3.1 for the training data. What can you say about the assumption of independent residuals? Repeat the same for the test data.

Tip

Plot the autocorrelation function of the residuals to validate the independence assumption.

# Compute the residuals for train and test data
residuals_train <- y_train3 - y_hat3_train
residuals_test <- y_test3 - y_hat3_test

# Plot residuals on train and test dataa
plot(residuals_train, type = "l", main = "Train Data residuals")
plot(residuals_test, type = "l", main = "Test Data residuals")
# Plot acf 
acf(residuals_train, main = "Train Data residuals")
acf(residuals_test, main = "Test Data residuals")

From the plots of acf for both train and test data, we can see that acf spikes far out of the threshold levels (represent the approximate 95% confidence interval under the null hypothesis that the data is uncorrelated) in the first 30 lags, which indicate the strong correlation between past and future data. Therefore, the assumption of independent residuals is wrong.

If all bars stay within the dashed lines, the series shows no significant autocorrelation in that lag.

4. Regularised time series regression and regression trees for bike rental data

In this section we will consider the time series nature of the data.

Problem 4.2

Add time series effects to your model by including some lagged values of the response as features. Use the first four hourly lags of log_cnt plus the 24th hourly lag as features, in addition to all other features in Problem 3.1. Fit the model using an L1 regularisation and find the optimal \(\lambda\) by applying the one-standard deviation rule when cross-validating the training data using 10 folds. Compute the RMSE (using the optimal \(\lambda\)) for the training and test data and compare to Problem 3.1. Are the residuals from this new model more adequate?

Tip

The function mutate() from the dplyr package is useful for adding columns to a data frame. Moreover, the function lags(x, k) lags the time series x by k steps.

Notice that some observations are lost when lagging, i.e. NA values are introduced. You can remove these observations from the dataset.

# Load dplyr library
library(dplyr)

Attaching package: 'dplyr'
The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':

    filter, lag
The following objects are masked from 'package:base':

    intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
# Create lag features
bike_data <- bike_data %>%
  mutate(
    lag1 = lag(log_cnt, 1),
    lag2 = lag(log_cnt, 2),
    lag3 = lag(log_cnt, 3),
    lag4 = lag(log_cnt, 4),
    lag24 = lag(log_cnt, 24)
  )

# Drop NA rows
bike_data <- na.omit(bike_data)

y_train <- bike_train_4.2$log_cnt
y_test <- bike_test_4.2$log_cnt

# Spline for hours
spline_train <- ns(bike_train_4.2$hour, df = 10, intercept = FALSE)
knots <- attr(spline_train, "knots")
spline_test <- ns(bike_test_4.2$hour, df = 10, knots = knots, intercept = FALSE)

# Design matrices
x_train <- cbind(
  1,
  spline_train,
  bike_train_4.2[, c("yr", "holiday", "workingday", "temp", "atemp", "hum", "windspeed",
                 "Spring", "Summer", "Fall", "Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat",
                 "cloudy", "light rain", "heavy rain",
                 "lag1", "lag2", "lag3", "lag4", "lag24")]
)

x_test <- cbind(
  1,
  spline_test,
  bike_test_4.2[, c("yr", "holiday", "workingday", "temp", "atemp", "hum", "windspeed",
                "Spring", "Summer", "Fall", "Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat",
                "cloudy", "light rain", "heavy rain",
                "lag1", "lag2", "lag3", "lag4", "lag24")]
)

# Fit L1
set.seed(0)
cv_L1_4 <- cv.glmnet(as.matrix(x_train), y_train, alpha = 1, nfolds = 10, intercept = FALSE)
lambda_best <- cv_L1_4$lambda.1se

# Predict in-sample
y_hat_train <- predict(cv_L1_4, newx = as.matrix(x_train), s = lambda_best)
RMSE_train <- sqrt(mean((y_train - y_hat_train)^2))
residuals_train <- y_train - y_hat_train
acf(residuals_train, main = "ACF of Training Residuals")
# Predict out-of-sample
y_hat_test <- predict(cv_L1_4, newx = as.matrix(x_test), s = lambda_best)
RMSE_test <- sqrt(mean((y_test - y_hat_test)^2))
residuals_test <- y_test - y_hat_test
acf(residuals_test, main = "ACF of Test Residuals")
cat("RMSE_train:", RMSE_train, "\n")
RMSE_train: 0.4360592 
cat("RMSE_test:", RMSE_test, "\n")
RMSE_test: 0.3732618 
cat("lambda_best:", lambda_best, "\n")
lambda_best: 0.007612828 
Problem 3.1 RMSE_train 0.7284213   RMSE test 0.7113729 
Problem 4.2 RMSE_train: 0.4360592  RMSE_test: 0.3732618

Based on RMSE and the shape of ACF plots, the model in 4.2 perform significantly better than 3.1’s. As the volume of the spikes in ACF of 4.2 is much lower, and closer to the thresholds, and it’s RMSE in both train and test data is only around half of that in 3.1.

Problem 4.4

Another alternative to the semi-parametric approach above is to fit a regression tree.

Using the training dataset from Problem 4.2 (that also includes lagged values of the response as features), fit a regression tree using the tree package. If you want, experiment with the settings to see how changing them affects the results.

library(tree)
#Creates a data frame with the response variable log_cnt and all predictors from x_train. This is required because tree() expects a formula interface or a data frame.
bike_train_4.2 <- data.frame(
  log_cnt = y_train,
  x_train
)
bike_test_4.2 <- data.frame(
  log_cnt = y_test,
  x_test
)
# Fit tree model
set.seed(0)
tree_model <- tree(log_cnt ~ ., data = bike_train_4.2)

y_hat_tree_train <- predict(tree_model, newdata = bike_train_4.2)
y_hat_tree_test <- predict(tree_model, newdata = bike_test_4.2)

RMSE_tree_train <- sqrt(mean((y_train - y_hat_tree_train)^2))
RMSE_tree_test <- sqrt(mean((y_test - y_hat_tree_test)^2))

cat("RMSE (Train):", RMSE_tree_train, "\n")
RMSE (Train): 0.5706015 
cat("RMSE (Test):", RMSE_tree_test, "\n")

5. Logistic regression and decision trees for classifying spam emails

The dataset spam_ham_emails.RData consists of \(n=4601\) spam (\(y=1\)) and ham (no spam, \(y=0\)) emails with corresponding 15 features2.

Most of the features are continuous real variables in the interval \([0, 100]\), with values corresponding to the percentage of occurrence of a specific word or character in the email. There are also a few features that capture the tendency to use many capital letters. The features are on different scales so we will standardise them to have zero mean and unit variance. The following code reads in the data (note that you have to change to the path were you stored the file!), standardises the features, and codes the response variable as a factor.

rm(list=ls()) # Remove variables

Spam_ham_emails['spam'] <- as.factor(Spam_ham_emails['spam'] == 1) # Changing from 1->TRUE, 0->FALSE # as.factor summarizes all categories and and their frequencies # logistic regression works well with factors
levels(Spam_ham_emails$spam) <- c("not spam", "spam") # change the name of levels from FALSE/TRUE by default to "not spam", "spam"

The response is the first column spam and we will use all the other features to predict if an email is a spam or ham. Let us first inspect the fraction of spam emails in the dataset.

cat("Percentage of spam:", 100*mean(Spam_ham_emails$spam == "spam"))
Percentage of spam: 39.40448

We now split the data using the createDataPartition() function in the caret package. The default method in caret is stratified sampling, which keeps the same fraction of spam and ham in both the training and test datasets. We use 75% of the data for training and 25% for testing.

set.seed(1234)
suppressMessages(library(caret))
train_obs <- createDataPartition(y = Spam_ham_emails$spam, p = .75, list = FALSE)
# split data into train and test, y =... preserves the class distribution (spam/not spam), p =... is the ratio of training set
train <- Spam_ham_emails[train_obs, ] # assign data to the set, train_obs = train data, - train_obs = test data
test <- Spam_ham_emails[-train_obs, ]
# Confirm both training and test are balanced with respect to spam emails
cat("Percentage of training data consisting of spam emails:", 
              100*mean(train$spam == "spam"), "\n")
Percentage of training data consisting of spam emails: 39.40887 
cat("Percentage of test data consisting of spam emails:", 
              100*mean(test$spam == "spam"))
Percentage of test data consisting of spam emails: 39.3913

The following code fits a logistic regression on the training data using the glm() function, predicts the test data following the rule if \(\mathrm{Pr}(y=1|\mathbf{x})>0.5 \Rightarrow y=1\), and computes the confusion matrix using the caret package.

glm_fit <- glm(spam ~ ., family = binomial, data = train) # Fits a logistic regression model using the training data
Warning: glm.fit: fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred
y_prob_hat_test <- predict(glm_fit, newdata = test, type = "response") # Uses the trained logistic model (glm_fit) to predict probabilities of being "spam" on the test set
threshold <- 0.5 # Predict spam if probability > threshold # Emails with predicted probability > 0.5 are classified as "spam", otherwise "not spam".
y_hat_test <- as.factor(y_prob_hat_test > threshold) # Converts predicted probabilities to class labels: TRUE becomes 1 (later "spam"), FALSE becomes 0 (later "not spam")
levels(y_hat_test) <- c("not spam", "spam") # Renames the factor levels from default "FALSE"/"TRUE" to "not spam"/"spam" to ensure consistency with test$spam, which uses those labels.
confusionMatrix(data = y_hat_test, test$spam, positive = "spam") # Generates a confusion matrix comparing: data = y_hat_test: your model’s predicted class labels, reference = test$spam: the actual class labels, positive = "spam" specifies that "spam" is the class of interest (important for precision, recall, F1 score, etc.).

Problem 5.2

Compute the accuracy, precision, sensitivity (recall), and specificity without using the confusionMatrix() function. Explain these four concepts in the context of the spam filter.

# extract values from confusion matrix
TP <- manual_confusion_matrix["spam", "spam"]
TN <- manual_confusion_matrix["not spam", "not spam"]
FP <- manual_confusion_matrix["spam", "not spam"]
FN <- manual_confusion_matrix["not spam", "spam"]
cat(" TP", TP, "\n","TN", TN, "\n","FP", FP, "\n","FN", FN)
 TP 388 
 TN 658 
 FP 39 
 FN 65
accuracy <- (TP+TN)/(TP+TN+FP+FN)
cat("accuracy", accuracy, "\n")
accuracy 0.9095652 
precision <- TP/(TP + FP)
cat("precision", precision, "\n")
precision 0.9086651 
sensitivity <- TP/(TP + FN)
cat("sensitivity", sensitivity, "\n")
sensitivity 0.8565121 
specificity <- TN/(TN + FP)
cat("specificity", specificity, "\n")
specificity 0.9440459

Accuracy = 0.9095652: overall, the model can detect spam emails correctly 90% of the times

Precision = 0.9086651: 90% of the emails that the model classifies as spam is indeed spam

Sensitivity = 0.8565121: 85% of the spam emails are successfully detected

Specificity = 0.9440459: the model can detect not spam emails correctly 94% of the times

Problem 5.3

Compute the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve using the pROC. Explain in detail what the ROC curve shows.

suppressMessages(library(pROC))
# Plot ROC curve
roc_curve <- roc(response = test$spam,
               predictor = y_prob_hat_test,
               levels = c("not spam", "spam"),
               direction = "<")
plot(roc_curve, col = "red", lwd = 2, main = "ROC Curve")
# Find best threshold and AUC as input for my comment below
cat("AUC", auc(roc_curve), "\n")
AUC 0.9650901 
best_threshold <- coords(roc_curve, x = "best", best.method = "youden", transpose = FALSE)
print(best_threshold)
  threshold specificity sensitivity
1 0.3979249   0.9124821   0.9028698

With AUC = 0.9650901, close to 1, we can conclude that using logistic regression method perform well in separating spam and not spam emails.

The ROC (Receiver operating characteristics) curve is ploted between the recall/true positive rate (x axis) and the false positive rate (y axis). It shows the trade off between 2 quantities as we vary the thresholdevaluated the model at different threshold, and the best threshold is at 0.3979249 (meaning if an email has more than 39,79% probability of being a spam email, it should be classified as spam). At this threshold, both specificity and sensitivity of the model is over 90%, indicating that its performance is also high.
